g.text: The origin sees roughly 1% of tile traffic - and that is the entire rendering design
Three services whose boundaries are forced by DATA SHAPE rather than by team structure, plus one path that is not a service at all.
Map rendering - note what is absent
client computes
(z, x, y) itself
NO server call
CDN edge
nearest PoP
HIT ~99% served from the edge.
The origin never hears about it.
MISS ~1% fetch from the object-storage
origin, cache at the edge, serve
object storage
Three properties make that possible, and all three have to hold:
tiles are IMMUTABLE
a given (z,x,y) never changes content, so an edge
can cache it indefinitely with no invalidation
protocol at all.
the URL is COMPUTABLE client-side
so there is no 'which tiles do I need?' round trip
on the most frequent operation in the product.
tiles are small and INDEPENDENT
so a viewport is a handful of parallel requests, and
a partially-loaded map still renders.
And the tile-serving path IS NOT A SERVICE AT ALL: no application logic on the read path, no database, and no request the
origin normally sees. Making it a service would put compute in front of data that never changes - the definition of pointless
work. Updating the map publishes a NEW VERSION PREFIX rather than invalidating anything, because purging 5.86 trillion objects
is not an operation anyone wants to attempt.
The two paths that are services
client -> LB -> NAVIGATION service compute-heavy, READ-ONLY
2. derive the endpoint routing tiles from their geohashes
3. route planner: load coarse tiles along the corridor
-> A* across tiles, stitching neighbours as it traverses
-> refine near the endpoints with fine-grained tiles
4. ETA service: per-segment time from live + historical traffic
5. ranker: order candidates by the user's filters
6. encode the polyline; assemble turn-by-turn instructions
Routing tiles come from OBJECT STORAGE, cached aggressively in the navigation
service's memory - deliberately not a database. There is no query to run: the
access pattern is 'give me tile 9q8yy at detail level 3', a key lookup for an
opaque binary blob. A database would add query planning, transactions and
indexing to serve GETs of immutable files.
And navigation is ONE service, not five. The route planner, shortest-path search,
ETA lookup and ranking all operate on the same in-memory routing tiles inside one
request's latency budget. Splitting them would mean shipping graph data between
services or re-loading tiles per hop - the same argument the stock exchange makes
about shared memory, at a much gentler latency scale.
client batches ~15 GPS samples (75 s of movement)
-> POST /v1/locations -> LB -> LOCATION INGEST write-only
-> 202 Accepted immediately <- ack BEFORE any storage work
-> async: append to Cassandra (user_id + day bucket)
-> async: publish to Kafka
|- traffic aggregator -> per-segment speed -> edge weights
|- road-detection pipeline (new roads, closures, one-ways)
+- analytics warehouse
Acknowledging BEFORE storing is the right call here, and it is worth defending
rather than treating as sloppiness. A GPS sample is worthless within a minute,
self-corrected by the next batch, and its purpose is STATISTICAL - traffic speed
is an aggregate over thousands of vehicles, so losing one vehicle's batch changes
no number anyone sees.
The ingest service also never READS. Coupling it to navigation would mean a
Cassandra write stall affecting route computation.
Geocoding is separate because it is a TEXT-SEARCH problem - fuzzy matching,
abbreviations, many languages - over a small dataset with a completely different
engine: an inverted index, not a graph.
Backpressure hits the navigation service's CPU - the only component doing real per-request work
location update batches
dropped at the ingest tier. Statistical, so losing a fraction changes no aggregate.
The cheapest possible saving.
alternative routes
return one route instead of three: ~3x less pathfinding for a modest product
degradation.
reroute recomputation for in-flight navigators
they already have a working route; a BETTER route is a nice-to-have.
long-distance route requests
queued or rate-limited before short ones, since their cost is far higher.
NEVER shed an initial route request, or tile serving
a user staring at a blank map, or unable to start navigating, experiences the product
as broken.
Tile serving essentially cannot be overloaded - the CDN absorbs it - and ingest is trivially parallel. Load is sharply diurnal
but GEOGRAPHICALLY STAGGERED: rush hour rolls around the planet, so global load is far flatter than any single region's, with
regional peaks about 5x the regional average.
The one place the CDN economics get uncomfortable
The ~99% hit rate holds because tile requests are extremely concentrated - cities, motorways, tourist sites. But the LONG TAIL
IS ENORMOUS: 4.4 trillion zoom-21 tiles exist and the overwhelming majority are requested approximately never. A user panning
across empty countryside generates a run of edge misses, each a fetch from object storage.
Two mitigations, both already in the design for other reasons: PREFETCH tiles adjacent to the viewport (the user is probably
about to pan there), and lean on UNIFORM-TILE DEDUPLICATION so an ocean tile is one cached object serving billions of
coordinates rather than billions of distinct cold objects.
Races - and how many of them resolve to 'nothing happens'
race
mechanism
what the loser sees
two clients request the same uncached tile
the CDN COLLAPSES concurrent origin requests
into one fetch
nothing - both get the tile and the origin sees one
request. Without collapsing, a viral location delivers
thousands of identical origin fetches.
a map version is published mid-session
new version, new path prefix; old tiles stay
valid and cached
nothing. THERE IS NO MOMENT OF INCONSISTENCY to
manage - which is the whole argument for versioning
over purging.
traffic data updates during a route search
edge weights are read ONCE at the start,
giving a consistent snapshot
a route computed against weights up to a few seconds
old. Re-reading mid-search could produce an internally
inconsistent path - worse than a slightly stale one.
two location batches arrive out of order
the Cassandra key is ((user_id, bucket), ts),
so each sample lands in its own position
nothing. APPEND-ONLY, TIMESTAMP-KEYED STORAGE MAKES
REORDERING A NON-ISSUE, which is why no sequencing is
needed on a 694k samples/sec path.
a user-requested reroute races an incident push
each route carries a version; the client takes
the higher one
one route is discarded, and both were valid - the
version just stops a stale push replacing a fresher
user-initiated route.
two aggregators compute one segment's speed
an idempotent overwrite of an aggregate over a
time window
nothing - both compute the same value from the same
window, which is why the aggregator needs no leader
election.
Degradation, in order of user impact - and note where the worst one is
ETA service down routes computed with static weights: directions CORRECT, times approximate. The ideal degradation
shape - lose the enhancement, keep the function.
traffic aggregator down weights go stale, so routes ignore new congestion. Degrades gradually rather than failing.
location ingest down traffic data stops improving. ZERO immediate user impact; the visible effect appears hours later.
geocoding down address search fails, but navigation between coordinates still works - so 'navigate to a dropped
pin' survives while 'navigate to an address' does not.
navigation service down no NEW routes. In-progress navigation continues, because the client already holds its full route
and instructions - deliberately not dependent on the server mid-journey.
CDN down the origin is hammered and rendering degrades badly. THE WORST FAILURE, and the mitigation is
multiple CDN providers with DNS failover.
Multi-region is genuinely easy here, because the data is geographic: tiles are global and edge-cached by nature, a region's
routing tiles are served from that region, and location history is homed regionally. THERE IS NO GLOBAL WRITE-CONSISTENCY
REQUIREMENT ANYWHERE IN THE SYSTEM - a striking contrast with the digital wallet, where multi-region is the hardest unsolved
problem.
What you'd revisit
the tile URL convention is effectively permanent
because clients compute (z,x,y) themselves, changing the scheme means old app versions keep requesting old URLs for years.
The honest position: this saves a round trip in exchange for a decision you cannot revisit.
'who is affected' by an incident is the least-solved piece
the multi-resolution tile approach is an approximation - it identifies users whose route MIGHT pass through an incident, then
must recompute to know. At millions of concurrent navigators, the recomputation cost of a major motorway closure is
substantial and unbudgeted here.
traffic data has a feedback loop nobody has modelled
routing everyone around congestion CREATES congestion on the alternative - and because the ETA model trains on observed
speeds that were themselves shaped by past routing decisions, the system is partly predicting its own behaviour. Real
deployments deliberately split traffic across alternatives to damp this; that mechanism is absent.
2.4 TB/day of precise movement traces, retained 'for traffic modelling'
aggregate speed per segment per time-of-day is a tiny fraction of that data, and it is what the product actually needs.
Retaining per-user traces indefinitely is a privacy liability well beyond the stated purpose, and no erasure path is
designed.
no offline-map story
the client holding its full route mid-journey is half of offline navigation; the other half is pre-downloading tiles and
routing tiles for a region and doing pathfinding on-device - a substantially different client architecture.
